title: Acts 10:1–23
context: Cornelius, a God-fearing Roman centurion in Caesarea who prays and gives generously, sees an angel who tells him to send for Peter in Joppa. The next day, while his messengers are on the way, Peter falls into a trance on a rooftop and sees a sheet full of unclean animals, with a voice telling him to kill and eat; when he refuses, the voice says not to call unclean what God has cleansed. As Peter ponders the vision, the Spirit tells him to go with the men without hesitation, and he hosts them and sets out the following day.

verses.text: Now there was a certain man in Caesarea, Cornelius by name, a centurion of what was called the Italian Regiment,
verses.arminianNotes: Cornelius is a centurion of the Italian cohort in Caesarea. Arminian readers see a Gentile soldier, an unlikely candidate for the next great step of the mission.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God choosing a Gentile household to open the door to the nations.

verses.text: a devout man, and one who feared God with all his house, who gave gifts for the needy generously to the people, and always prayed to God.
verses.arminianNotes: He is devout, fears God with his household, gives alms, and prays continually. Arminian commentators often see prevenient grace already at work, drawing him toward God before he heard the gospel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see God’s preparatory work in a man he intends to save, while noting that he still needed to hear of Christ (11:14).

verses.text: At about the ninth hour of the day, he clearly saw in a vision an angel of God coming to him and saying to him, “Cornelius!”
verses.arminianNotes: At three in the afternoon he sees an angel in a vision. Arminian readers see God responding to a seeker’s prayers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God initiating contact at the hour of prayer.

verses.text: He, fastening his eyes on him and being frightened, said, “What is it, Lord?” He said to him, “Your prayers and your gifts to the needy have gone up for a memorial before God.
verses.arminianNotes: His prayers and alms have gone up as a memorial before God. Arminian expositors see God noticing sincere devotion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see God remembering what he himself prompted, without treating it as earning salvation.

verses.text: Now send men to Joppa, and get Simon, who is also called Peter.
verses.arminianNotes: He is to send to Joppa for Simon Peter. Arminian readers see God using a human messenger even when an angel is present.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the angel directing him to the preached word, the ordinary means of salvation.

verses.text: He is staying with a tanner named Simon, whose house is by the seaside.
verses.arminianNotes: Peter is staying with Simon the tanner by the sea. Arminian commentators see precise directions given.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see providence in every detail.

verses.text: When the angel who spoke to him had departed, Cornelius called two of his household servants and a devout soldier of those who waited on him continually.
verses.arminianNotes: Cornelius calls two servants and a devout soldier. Arminian readers see immediate obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a household already shaped by his faith.

verses.text: Having explained everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.
verses.arminianNotes: He explains everything and sends them to Joppa. Arminian expositors see his openness to God’s direction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see God moving events toward the meeting.

verses.text: Now on the next day as they were on their journey and got close to the city, Peter went up on the housetop to pray at about noon.
verses.arminianNotes: At noon the next day Peter goes up on the roof to pray. Arminian readers see prayer as the place where God redirects his servants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God timing Peter’s vision with the messengers’ approach.

verses.text: He became hungry and desired to eat, but while they were preparing, he fell into a trance.
verses.arminianNotes: He becomes hungry and falls into a trance. Arminian commentators see God speaking through ordinary needs.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see God preparing his servant’s heart for a new step.

verses.text: He saw heaven opened and a certain container descending to him, like a great sheet let down by four corners on the earth,
verses.arminianNotes: He sees heaven opened and a sheet let down. Arminian readers see a vision that comes from God, not from Peter’s imagination.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see revelation from heaven overturning settled assumptions.

verses.text: in which were all kinds of four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, reptiles, and birds of the sky.
verses.arminianNotes: It contains all kinds of animals, clean and unclean. Arminian expositors see a picture of all nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see the food laws, which separated Israel from the nations, about to be set aside.

verses.text: A voice came to him, “Rise, Peter, kill and eat!”
verses.arminianNotes: “Rise, Peter, kill and eat!” Arminian readers see a command that challenges Peter’s habits.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s authority to redefine what is clean.

verses.text: But Peter said, “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.”
verses.arminianNotes: Peter refuses because he has never eaten anything unclean. Arminian commentators see sincere scruples that God must correct.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see that even an apostle needed his thinking reformed by revelation.

verses.text: A voice came to him again the second time, “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.”
verses.arminianNotes: “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.” Arminian readers see God declaring Gentiles welcome in his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s cleansing as his sovereign act, which no human may contradict.

verses.text: This was done three times, and immediately the thing was received up into heaven.
verses.arminianNotes: This happens three times. Arminian expositors recall Peter’s threefold denial and threefold restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see emphasis on certainty.

verses.text: Now while Peter was very perplexed in himself what the vision which he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood before the gate,
verses.arminianNotes: While Peter is perplexed, Cornelius’s men arrive. Arminian readers see God answering Peter’s question through events.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see providence and revelation meeting at the same moment.

verses.text: and called and asked whether Simon, who was also called Peter, was lodging there.
verses.arminianNotes: They ask whether Simon Peter is staying there. Arminian commentators see the moment of decision approaching.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see God’s plan unfolding step by step.

verses.text: While Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men seek you.
verses.arminianNotes: The Spirit tells Peter that three men are looking for him. Arminian readers see the Spirit guiding personally.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Spirit directing the mission to the Gentiles.

verses.text: But arise, get down, and go with them, doubting nothing; for I have sent them.”
verses.arminianNotes: He must go with them without doubting, for the Spirit sent them. Arminian expositors see a call to trust that overrides old barriers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see the Spirit as the true sender of the mission.

verses.text: Peter went down to the men, and said, “Behold, I am he whom you seek. Why have you come?”
verses.arminianNotes: Peter goes down and asks why they have come. Arminian readers see willingness to engage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see obedience following revelation.

verses.text: They said, “Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man and one who fears God, and well spoken of by all the nation of the Jews, was directed by a holy angel to invite you to his house, and to listen to what you say.”
verses.arminianNotes: They describe Cornelius as righteous, God-fearing, and well spoken of by the Jews. Arminian commentators see a good reputation preparing the way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see God’s instruction that Cornelius should hear Peter’s words.

verses.text: So he called them in and provided a place to stay. On the next day Peter arose and went out with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.
verses.arminianNotes: Peter invites them in as guests, and the next day goes with some brothers from Joppa. Arminian readers see hospitality to Gentiles as the first sign of change.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Peter bringing witnesses, which will matter in chapter 11.
